questions.question: Why is DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL a broken HPA signal for LLM serving with vLLM?
options: It measures VRAM allocation, which vLLM always keeps near 100% regardless of load
It is a duty-cycle metric that reads 100% whether there are 10 or 100 concurrent requests
It only works with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and not H100s
It requires a custom Prometheus exporter that conflicts with vLLM's metrics endpoint
questions.explanation: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL is a duty-cycle metric — it reports whether the GPU was doing work each sampling interval, not how many requests it is serving. 100% could mean 10 or 100 requests. Scaling on duty cycle is scaling blindly.

questions.question: What is gang scheduling and what failure mode does KAI Scheduler prevent?
options: Scheduling all pods of a job atomically, preventing the partial-allocation trap where 7 of 8 GPUs idle
Grouping GPU nodes into gangs to share NVLink bandwidth more efficiently
Scheduling by priority queue so high-priority jobs preempt low-priority without waiting
Batching multiple small inference requests together to saturate a single GPU
questions.explanation: Gang scheduling means all N pods of a distributed job must start together or none start at all. KAI Scheduler prevents the partial-allocation trap: without it, 7 of 8 required GPUs could start, sit idle, and burn money waiting for the last one.

questions.question: What is the safe Karpenter consolidation policy for GPU inference node pools in 2026?
options: consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized with consolidateAfter: 0s
consolidationPolicy: WhenEmpty with consolidateAfter: 1h
consolidationPolicy: Never — GPU nodes should never be consolidated
consolidationPolicy: WhenUnderutilized with consolidateAfter: 30m
questions.explanation: WhenEmpty with consolidateAfter: 1h allows Karpenter to reclaim truly empty nodes after an hour but never evicts running GPU workloads. The default WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized will terminate running GPU nodes mid-inference, causing request failures and model reload delays.

questions.question: What are the two correct replacement HPA signals for vLLM scaling instead of GPU duty-cycle utilization?
options: VRAM usage and CPU utilization
Queue depth and KV cache utilization
Network throughput and disk I/O
Model load time and active connection count
questions.explanation: Queue depth (requests waiting for prefill) measures actual demand, not idle-vs-busy. KV cache utilization measures memory pressure on the decode pool. Both are inference-specific and avoid the problems of DCGM duty-cycle and memory-usage signals.

questions.question: Karpenter provisions GPU nodes in approximately how long compared to Cluster Autoscaler?
options: Karpenter: ~5-10 minutes vs Cluster Autoscaler: ~10-15 minutes
Karpenter: ~45-60 seconds vs Cluster Autoscaler: ~90-120 seconds
Karpenter: ~10-15 seconds vs Cluster Autoscaler: ~60-90 seconds
Both tools provision at the same speed; the difference is scheduling quality
questions.explanation: The lesson states Karpenter provisions nodes in ~45-60 seconds versus Cluster Autoscaler's ~90-120 seconds for GPU nodes — roughly 40% faster. This matters when a request arrives at a cold cluster.

questions.question: In a disaggregated prefill/decode architecture, why should prefill pods and decode pods have separate HPA configurations?
options: They run on different Kubernetes namespaces and cannot share an HPA
Prefill is compute-bound (scales on queue depth) and decode is memory-bound (scales on KV cache pressure)
Kubernetes only supports one HPA per deployment, so they must be split
Prefill pods require GPU while decode pods can run on CPU, requiring different node pools
questions.explanation: Prefill is compute-bound and scales on queue depth; decode is memory-bound and scales on KV cache utilization. Using a single HPA in front of both would pick the wrong signal for at least one role.
